overview: The Solomon Islands contain many distinct societies. A regional comparison of shell-working and adornment reveals skilled manufacture and different local meanings; it does not imply a single ancient civilization.

items.text: Makers ground, polished and drilled shell discs, then strung them with plant fibre. Labour and visual qualities both contributed to their value.
Wooden ear ornaments could hold cut shell inlay secured with paste from the parinarium nut. Material contrast made intricate designs visible.
Canoe-prow figures are called nguzunguzu around Roviana Lagoon and toto isu around Marovo Lagoon. Preserving local names avoids erasing differences within New Georgia.
Shell ornaments communicated status and could relate to shell-money exchange. Their meanings combined appearance, ceremony and relationships with ancestors.

sources.title: Sylvia Cockburn, Body Adornment in Solomon Islands
sources.note: Shell bead manufacture; nguzunguzu terminology; shell inlay and nut paste; regional variation. Essay credits Solomon Islands National Museum consultations.
